newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu under intense pressure to quit.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu under intense pressure to quit.

text.p: Zaire's veteran strongman Mobutu Sese Seko faced intense pressure to quit on Friday as the international community looked for a negotiated transition to democracy in the sprawling Central African nation.
Rebels who control half Zaire including its economic heartland have paused in their relentless advance and have given the ailing Zairean president until the weekend to signal a willingness to quit.
In Geneva, U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan urged the two sides to return to the negotiating table.
On the humanitarian front, the U.N. said it flew 240 displaced Zaireans to the eastern border town of Goma in a test run for the repatriation of up to 100,000 Rwandan refugees.
"The scenario is very fluid and anything can happen," Annan told a Geneva news conference.
"We are also all aware that there is tremendous pressure on President Mobutu to step down," he said, loosely outlining scenarios in which Mobutu could bow out with dignity.

Annan urged the warring sides to resume peace talks. "I'd hope that when they come back together, they will be discussing transitional arrangements and eventually national elections for the selection of a leader of the country," he said.
Mobutu, 66, has held sway over Africa's third largest nation since a 1965 coup. He had prostate cancer surgery in August.

Laurent Kabila's rebels took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis. They won their greatest prize to date on Wednesday, seizing Zaire's second city, the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi.
Representatives of Mobutu and the rebels ended a first round of talks in South Africa last week recognising the need for talks on a peaceful settlement and a truce.

South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki who hosted the talks said in Washington on Thursday that he hoped negotiations would resume early next week. He said he expected the question of Mobutu's future to be on the agenda.
Kinshasa, rocked by Wednesday clashes between Mobutu security forces and supporters of ousted prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi, enjoyed a second day of calm on Friday.
Security forces patrolled the capital's streets on Friday as usual as the city waited for Mobutu's new emergency rule prime minister General Likulia Bolongo to announce his government.
Opposition leader Tshisekedi, shunted aside by Mobutu after under a week in the job, has accused his arch-foe of treason and urged Zaireans to step up pressure to force him from power.
The governor of the southern mining province of Shaba, waiting for word from Kabila on his future, said on Friday it was time for the president to go.
"Mobutu must retire now because of his health rather than continuing a war that is futile," Kyungu wa Kumwanza said in Lubumbashi, Shaba's capital.
State-owned copper and cobalt producer Gecamines, which closed its Lubumbashi head offices this week fearing fighting, said it would resume normal business on Monday.

Former colonial power Belgium and the United States have said Mobutu's time has passed. France, a long-time Mobutu ally, has called for an orderly transition but has cast doubts on Kabila's democratic credentials.
With many of Mobutu's one-time allies urging him to stand aside, South Africa's Mbeki said there was no suggestion as yet that the Zairean president would want to seek asylum.
Asked about South Africa's response to any request, he replied: "I don't think we would respond negatively."
